children.text:
Credentials published on GitHub are not automatically revoked - what happens is at the discretion of the provider, for precisely this reason.

For example AWS applies a “quarantine” policy that prevents some specific actions[1].

Allowing anyone to report a potentially compromised key is one thing, but allowing anyone to unilaterally revoke a token is another.

1. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/refere...

Is that system made by a supervillain or a mad scientist? But such system can go amok for any reason. Anyway revocation is already possible by publication on github, telling to GPT or sending an email to webmaster.

Are you really unable to imagine a situation where financial or physical harm is caused by a system abruptly being shut down by a credential revocation, triggered by a random person on the internet?

Be serious.
Given they found a secret key in a public place? No that’s not malicious and it would be odd for a serious organisation to be upset someone immediately invalidated it.

And the whitehack hackers finding keys should do what, exactly?

Unilaterally decide they should be revoked, without contacting the owner?

And that’s not malicious?
It for whitehat third parties who discover unprotected keys obviously people intentionally stealing keys will not revoke them generally.

Think that through - the person who stole the key has the decision to use it or revoke it through this hypothetical system.

If they are acting maliciously, they will take the choice that most hurts you and/or benefits them.

If the key is useless to them and revoking it hurts you, then they would do that.

If the key wasn’t useless to them, then… they would just use it and not revoke it?
In this case you'd probably prefer your key to be disabled rather than spending $$$ on tokens for everyone else
That just turns a credential leak into a denial of service - one that can be triggered from anywhere.

I think every API key system should have endpoint "invalidate_api_key" this way whitehat hackers or the party who stored them could invalidate all keys in the case they leak. Now it is race against the time, and everybody got email, and everyone must act themselves.

children.text:
Yeah, it's very confusing especially if you're not in the loop and their docs were only updated recently and was confusing during the v1 -> v2 transition weeks / months ago.

So far, "OpenCode" has gone through several possible definitions:

- OpenCode Terminal / CLI - This is what you get normally. Runs a service in the background and the CLI is your interface.

- OpenCode Desktop - Instead of a CLI, you get a desktop interface.

Most users usually stop here. You just install the app and you connect wherever.

So there's the services where they both make money and make things easier for users:

- OpenCode Console - Basically the serving platform for both Zen and Go, and has expanded to a hosted inference gateway and somewhat similar to OpenRouter or a managed LiteLLM. Has the option to BYOK if you have existing AI platform accounts so it charges those instead of Zen, and that's what got compromised.

- OpenCode Zen - the API service they host if you want to get access to providers but don't want to pay individually per API platform. Similar to OpenRouter. I noticed they're kinda slowly dropping the Zen moniker.

- OpenCode Go - the subscription service that they host that features open weight models and select low-cost models from frontier labs. Has different policies when it comes to privacy and retention compared to Zen.

- OpenCode Black - a limited-time, limited access subscription service that grants access to frontier models. Not sure if this is still alive or not.

children.text: As a philosopher^H person on twitter once said: "If you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." OpenCode has some pedigree here.

To clarify something that the OpenCode team has done a bad job of clarifying:

The leak was for something called 'OpenCode Console', which is distinct and separate from the OpenCode coding agent. If you're just using the coding agent, you're not affected. 'OpenCode Console' is a service that is similar to OpenRouter, but is much less widely used.

The name 'OpenCode Console' is super confusing, because one might think it means the CLI coding agent. It does not. 'OpenCode Console' has nothing to do with the CLI/TUI coding agent, nor the desktop app version.

The situation is made worse by the fact that 'OpenCode Console' barely has any documentation online, and the official leak announcement does not make the distinction clear at all. The OpenCode team did a terrible job of communicating this, and that's on them.

Today is a bad day for people using 'OpenCode Console'. But most people, probably the vast majority of OpenCode users who are reading this, are not using 'OpenCode Console'.

A "distillation attack" is when someone tries to extract training data from a closed source model through the API of the Big Ai labs. Frontier model traces can be used to train other models with less effort. We don't use the word "attack" when a company does this with their own models or when we use open weights as the teacher model. This is often used to help train flash and smaller models from the mega models. The technique is used widely throughout industry.

We do not know if that is what the hacked API keys were used for. Could be distillation, could be API reselling. We will need more transparency into the nature of the requests made by the attacker. I would like to see an open dataset of the queries made with the compromised keys. All of them as originally made, not aggregate stats or another METR report.

The keys could have also been used to resell API access on the black market, again, we need good transparency to know. Considering the upstream parties involved, getting the distillation narrative out there early, without evidence, does fit a larger pattern we have seen from them this year.
